title: Frame Rates
principle: Keep game speed independent of how many frames are drawn
why: His NES/SNES games counted screen interrupts as time, so 50 fps PAL versions ran 5/6 as fast; from the N64 on, drawing fewer frames while running as intended caused less jarring tradeoffs. Dropping frames is not slowdown.
how: Decouple game logic timing from display refresh so frame drops or regional refresh rates don't change game speed.
anti_pattern: Tying game speed to a refresh rate that differs by region or platform.
example: NES/SNES PAL ports at 5/6 speed.
quote: In other words, porting games to PAL caused them to run 5/6 as fast.

title: Down with Lag!
principle: Use Game Mode and disable picture processing on displays
why: Display latency comes from post-processing that improves picture quality; Game Mode or Low Latency Mode bypasses it. At 60 fps every 16.67 ms is a frame of delay.
how: Switch test and play TVs to Game Mode or Low Latency Mode, or turn off all picture-enhancing settings, and prefer TVs with low listed display time.
anti_pattern: Leaving TV post-processing on for gameplay.
quote: With a 60 fps video output, a delay of 16.67 ms equates to one frame.

title: Draw the Light, Not the Asset
principle: Favor cheap techniques so more objects fit on screen
why: Shaders and post-processing can add detail on powerful machines, but that luxury is rare; the less you process an object, the more of it you can put on screen.
how: Achieve lighting and color variation in the asset itself where possible rather than relying on heavy per-object processing.
anti_pattern: Relying on expensive shaders when the hardware budget is tight.
quote: In terms of hardware performance, the less we process an object, the more of it we can put on screen.

title: Giving "Weight" to Buttons
principle: Configure analog stick tilt sensitivity per console
why: Each console's analog stick is slightly different, so the lowest value at which tilt is detected must be configured every time.
how: Set and test the minimum detected stick tilt separately for each platform or controller you support.
anti_pattern: One stick-sensitivity value for every console.
quote: Tilt sensitivity— the lowest value at which stick tilt is detected— is something we have to configure every time.

title: Name Files Logically
principle: Order name parts so sorting groups related files
why: With 'Attack' or 'Special' first and numbers for strength, moves stay together sorted from neutral to tilt to smash; direction-first names like 'SAttack' or word-based strengths would make a mess when sorted.
how: Use category, then direction (N/Hi/S/Lw, Air), then numbers for strength or sequence, and check folders sort sensibly.
anti_pattern: Putting modifiers before the category, or using words for strength.
example: Super Smash Bros. labels: Attack11-13, AttackS4, AttackAirF, SpecialHi.
quote: If we called them "SAttack" or "HiAttack," with the direction coming first... It would just make a huge mess when you sorted them all.

title: Name Files Logically
principle: Keep labels concise but readable at a glance
why: Someone seeing a name for the first time should know what it's for; names that are too short are easy to type but hard to understand.
how: Pick names that balance brevity with clarity, and test them on someone new to the project.
anti_pattern: Cryptic abbreviations.
quote: Keep your development file names and labels concise and easy to understand!

title: Name Files Logically
principle: Avoid romanized native-language words in shared file names
why: On bigger projects, romanized Japanese makes things harder for people who don't speak the language, and overseas teams joining later may not understand it.
how: Name files in English whenever other or international teams might work on the project.
anti_pattern: Romanized Japanese file names.
quote: Remember: it's not just you who needs to understand your game.

title: Distinguishing Between Major and Minor Elements
principle: Build LOD only when the performance gain justifies the labor.
why: LOD swaps in lower-polygon assets with distance, but it's labor-intensive.
how: Estimate the performance gain against the authoring cost before committing to LOD models.
anti_pattern: Building LOD by default.
quote: But implementing this is labor-intensive, so the performance benefit needs to be worth it.

title: Making Your Game Easy to Tune
principle: Separate every tunable value from code into designer-editable parameters.
why: Hard-coding means diving into code for every tweak, causing real problems; parameters let designers make the same code behave very differently.
how: Have programmers read values like attack power from a parameter table kept in a separate spreadsheet.
anti_pattern: Writing tunable numbers directly into code.
example: A move with attack power 10 stored as a parameter.
quote: You could say the code is the bones, and the parameters are the muscles.

title: Making Your Game Easy to Tune
principle: Hide rarely used parameters and link related ones with formulas.
why: Hiding reduces human error and surfaces the important values; formulas keep related values in relative balance.
how: Collapse low-frequency fields in the editor, and define dependent values, such as one move at 1/2 another's power.
example: Smash Bros. attack parameters in Excel.
quote: This helps reduce human error and makes it easier to find the important values, so hiding the parameters you don't use often is an effective approach.

title: Making Your Game Easy to Tune
principle: Push parameter changes to all test builds with one button.
why: Tuning is where you iterate most; ten-minute conversions plus reboots on early Smash games made every tweak costly.
how: Build a tool, such as a spreadsheet add-in, that converts parameters and updates every active dev kit in one press.
anti_pattern: Slow conversions and hand-edited text files.
example: Original Smash and Melee versus Wii U/3DS onward with Bandai Namco Studios.
quote: This is the area where you'll likely need to iterate the most, so make sure your team can do so as efficiently as possible.

title: Kirby Air Ride
principle: Create variety through parameters on one shared behavior
why: All Air Ride machines feel totally different yet share the same underlying behavior, so reworked code let the team change characteristics by tweaking a few numbers.
how: Implement one movement model (plus a few true types, like star vs. bike) and express each vehicle or character as a parameter set that the designer writes and tunes.
example: Kirby Air Ride machines
quote: Thanks to our reworked game code, we were able to change characteristics just by tweaking a few numbers.

title: Put Parameters in Brackets
principle: Keep tunable values in an external table, not in code
why: If parameters are hard-coded, every adjustment must go through a programmer, yet parameters keep being tweaked for balance to the very end, after the programmer's job is done.
how: Create a reference table separate from the code that planners can adjust at any time, covering values like walking speed and special-move speeds.
anti_pattern: Writing parameters directly into the game code.
quote: In other words, we create a reference table separate from the code, which the planner can adjust at any point.

title: Learn to Count Frames!
principle: Specify timing in frames and verify the build by feel
why: Directors briefing the team with precise frame assignments must be able to count frames, and even correct specs can be broken by code or data errors.
how: Write exact frame numbers into move and animation specs, then play each move and investigate when it feels off.
anti_pattern: Assigning frame counts you can't actually feel.
quote: Even once you successfully implement the right frame counts, you may sometimes still end up with errors in the code or data.

title: Loading Screens
principle: Don't tie presentation length to development-build load times
why: Load times usually get optimized and shortened between development and release.
how: Use a reusable indicator that can appear for any duration, and only use load-masking transitions that still work if final loads are shorter.
anti_pattern: Transitions timed to today's slow dev loads.
example: The first Resident Evil's door animation hid loading so well that an icon would ruin the illusion.
quote: And so, you may not always want to make loading screens depend on presentation.

title: Units of Speed
principle: Build to real-world scale to use real speeds as-is
why: When characters and environments are defined in real units, real-life speeds can be used directly, which is much easier to understand.
how: Model characters and environments at real scale; switch to distance per frame where the game needs it.
quote: As long as characters and environments were defined in real-life units of measurement, we could use real speeds as-is in the game.

title: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking
principle: Test timing-based systems on the production hardware before release
why: He never tested on the production handheld; likely due to a processing-speed difference, the Mushi gets hungry faster than planned and puts unintended stress on players.
how: Before release, run hunger, fatigue and growth timers on the final hardware and compare their rates with the design values.
anti_pattern: Shipping having tested only on a development board.
example: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking's Mushi almost always wants food.
quote: Before it was done, I never got the chance to test the game out on the production handheld. As a result, there's an issue in the final version.

title: Emphasizing Text
principle: Let translators edit text-effect scripting for each language
why: Different languages have different styles of emphasis, so native speakers should decide what presentation reads naturally.
how: Store effect tags in the localizable script so translators can add, move or remove emphasis without developer help.
anti_pattern: Hardcoding text effects where only developers can change them.
quote: It's best to let native speakers from each country consider natural presentation, which is exactly why you want to make it so that translators can edit the scripting themselves.

title: The Family Computer (and the NES)
principle: Pack more game into tight budgets through technical skill
why: Mario Bros. was 24 KB and Super Mario Bros. 40 KB; that modest difference allowed for a lot more game thanks to shocking technical skill.
how: When storage is limited, push craft and technique to deliver more content instead of assuming you need more space.
example: Mario Bros. (24 KB) vs. Super Mario Bros. (40 KB).
quote: The technical skill packed into these tiny ROMs was frankly shocking.

title: The Family Computer (and the NES)
principle: Deliver visuals, sound, smooth motion, easy controls and fun together
why: The Famicom felt like a breath of fresh air because it combined gorgeous graphics, memorable sound, smooth processing, an easy controller and an affordable price, and best of all its games were fun.
how: Check each of these fronts in your game, including smooth animation instead of sprites that jump between frames as they walk.
example: Famicom vs. 1983 games with single-color blobs that jumped between frames.
quote: Best of all, the games were fun.

title: An Up-Close Look at Smash Bros. Stages
principle: Budget stage art for the worst-case load at target frame rate
why: Ultimate's stages had to run on Switch with eight fighters on-screen at 60 fps, which really didn't leave much leeway.
how: Profile each stage with the maximum number of characters active and keep its art within that budget.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's roughly 115 base stages.
quote: Making them work on Nintendo Switch with eight fighters on-screen at 60 frames per second really didn't give us much leeway.

title: Development Secrets of the Original Kirby
principle: Build similar characters from shared, flipped sprite parts
why: Kirby was largely designed for 512 kilobits (64 KB), so Waddle Dee and Waddle Doo share a back half: two characters in the ROM space of 1.5.
how: Mirror one image to animate (Gordo), reuse parts across variants (Kracko's eye for Kracko Jr.), and cap limb frames (Poppy Bros. Sr.: three leg and two head patterns).
example: Kirby's Dream Land: Waddle Dee/Waddle Doo, Gordo, Kracko, and the flip-friendly "M" on the Maxim Tomato.
quote: To be blunt, I wanted to make two characters using the ROM space of only 1.5.

title: Development Secrets of the Original Kirby
principle: Fake costly systems with hand-authored patterns when processing is scarce
why: Kirby's enemies had no terrain collision; their movement was authored to match the background, which was wasteful to make but light on processing, invaluable on Game Boy, and kept Cappy bouncy.
how: Script fixed enemy paths that mimic falls, ledges and water slowdown instead of running per-frame collision checks.
example: Kirby's Dream Land: Coner, Waddle Dee and Cappy movement patterns.
quote: Mainly, it was light on processing power. This was an invaluable benefit when working with the Game Boy.

title: Super Smash Bros. Brawl
principle: Match synchronous online players within the same local region
why: Smash needs fully synchronous communication, unlike asynchronous games like Mario Kart, so lag makes it choppy unless players are close.
how: For real-time synchronous games, matchmake within the same region rather than just the same country.
example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl online vs. Mario Kart.
quote: it works best sticking to not just your own country, but even your own local region within it.

title: Family BASIC
principle: Use built-in assets so scarce resources go to behavior
why: With only 2 KB of program space, coding your own pixel art would use it all up; Family BASIC's character presets made moving characters easy.
how: When memory or time is tight, use presets or placeholder art and spend your budget on movement and logic.
example: Family BASIC presets: Mario, Pauline and Luigi's palette.

title: Game Demos
principle: Strip spoiler data from pre-release demos, then retest thoroughly
why: People can and likely will find spoiler data left in a demo, and removing data greatly increases the chance of something breaking.
how: Keep spoiler content in separable files so it can be removed cleanly, audit the demo build, and run full QA after removal.
anti_pattern: Shipping a demo build with leftover spoiler data.

title: Super Smash Bros. for 3DS / Wii U
principle: Treat a stable 60 FPS as a must; pare content until it holds
why: Many 3DS games ran at 30 FPS or dropped stereoscopic 3D. Sakurai considered 60 FPS essential, so content was cut back until four-player matches with 3D ran smoothly.
how: Set the frame-rate target at the start, and when the weaker platform can't hold it, cut or simplify features (e.g., a two-character fighter) instead of lowering the target.
anti_pattern: Dropping to 30 FPS or removing a headline feature like 3D to fit everything in.
example: Smash for 3DS ran four players, stereoscopic 3D, items, Pokémon and Assist Trophies at 60 FPS. Ice Climbers, controlling two at once, was too much for the 3DS.
quote: I considered 60 FPS gameplay to be an absolute must, so we pared things down until that was realized.

title: Bug Testing Never Ends
principle: Target bug testing at likely contradiction points instead of brute-forcing combinations
why: With 89 fighters there are about 8,000 pairings before moves, items, players, stages and spirits are multiplied in, so testing everything is impossible. Bugs cluster where systems fight over control.
how: Test first where one entity forcibly controls another (grabs and throws, especially on a target mid special move), scene-changing super moves, extreme or V-shaped terrain, and modifier systems.
anti_pattern: Brute-force testing every combination with no prioritization.
example: Smash Ultimate: grabbing a fighter in the middle of a special move, Final Smashes with scene changes, Stage Builder V-shaped terrain, Spirits.

title: Bug Testing Never Ends
principle: Re-run broad checks after every bug fix before releasing the patch
why: Fixing one bug can introduce others ("enbugging"), so a fix can't simply ship right away.
how: Pair each fix with a regression pass over related systems and only then release the patch.
anti_pattern: Pushing a hotfix out immediately without re-checking.
quote: That's because fixing one bug might introduce others. This is sometimes called "enbugging."

title: Unexpected Results
principle: Re-verify difficulty after optimization when game speed tracks processing speed
why: In Meteos, game speed was directly tied to processing speed, so late optimization sped the game up and made it harder than intended, after tuning was done.
how: Identify any timing tied to processing speed and replay difficulty-critical content on the final optimized build before release.
anti_pattern: Treating smoother performance as purely a win when it also changes game speed.
example: Meteos: some planets' sequences became tough to finish in the time allotted.

title: Unexpected Results
principle: Do final tuning checks on the real production unit, not a dev board
why: Sakurai tuned Mushiking on a roughly one-square-meter custom dev board and never played the actual unit. On the production hardware, the Mushi got hungry faster than expected.
how: Before sign-off, play the finished game on retail hardware and compare timing-sensitive values against your dev setup.
anti_pattern: Tuning exclusively on development hardware.
example: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking.

title: Billboards
principle: Mix billboards with 3D parts to make simple objects cheaply
why: A single image can stand in for a whole object, and a billboard body can carry 3D-modeled details.
how: Billboard simple round or distant objects, and attach modeled parts where depth matters.
anti_pattern: Using billboards for objects that the camera circles closely.
example: Super Mario 64's rolling iron balls, and King Bob-omb's billboard body with 3D eyes and crown.

title: Fighter Reveal Videos
principle: Capture trailer gameplay with replay and debug camera tools
why: Smash's gameplay segments are recorded by dev team members using debug and replay features to find the best camera angles, then repeatedly checked and restructured.
how: Build replay playback with a free debug camera so trailer shots can be re-framed and re-shot from recorded matches.
example: Super Smash Bros. — fighter reveal gameplay segments
quote: They capture footage using debug and replay features to find the best camera angles.

title: How Multiple People Work on One File
principle: Track all game files on a server with lock-edit-upload-unlock
why: A large game has tens of thousands to millions of files and can have hundreds of people editing them, so you need a tool that stops two people from editing the same file at once.
how: Put every file under a management tool: editing a file locks it, and uploading the finished edit back to the server unlocks it.
anti_pattern: Sharing files by hand with no locking or tracking.
quote: When someone's editing a file, that file gets locked.

title: How Multiple People Work on One File
principle: Merge simultaneous edits to big files and resolve leftovers manually
why: Letting only one person work on a particularly large file is inefficient, and conflicting uploads happen anyway.
how: Allow concurrent edits on large files, let the tool compare and stitch the edits together, and have someone fix any discrepancies the merge can't resolve.
anti_pattern: Keeping a huge shared file locked to one person while others wait.

title: How Multiple People Work on One File
principle: Expect edits to get reverted and recover them from version history
why: Reversion, where changes vanish and the file returns to its pre-edit state, is a common occurrence even though the tools should work in theory.
how: When a change goes missing, go back a version: the tool backs up every edit, so the lost work can often be retrieved.
anti_pattern: Assuming the management tool makes lost changes impossible.
quote: There shouldn't be any issues, in theory— but in practice, it's a constant source of headaches.

title: Long Ago, Numbers Were Used to Draw Pixel Art
principle: Stack two 1-bit layers for three colors plus transparency
why: Overlaying two same-sized pixel layers gives four combinations per pixel: both empty, first filled, second filled, or both filled.
how: In tight-memory or retro formats, store each sprite as two bitplanes and map the four combinations to transparent plus three colors.
example: NES-style three-color sprites.

title: Long Ago, Numbers Were Used to Draw Pixel Art
principle: Compress repeated runs instead of storing every pixel value
why: Writing a run as a value and a count is much shorter than writing every value out.
how: Encode runs of identical data as value-times-count, such as 0x8 instead of 00000000.

title: Long Ago, Numbers Were Used to Draw Pixel Art
principle: Plan pixel art on a grid before converting it to data
why: Without graphics tools, drawing on graph paper first and counting out values afterward was the common way to get correct data.
how: Lay out the image on a grid first, then derive the values row by row.
example: Sakurai used a cross as a guide and estimated values on a borrowed pocket computer.
quote: Everyone used data—numbers, that is— to enter the value of each pixel.

title: Randomness Spices Games Up
principle: Seed random values with an indefinite input like the clock
why: Computers can't produce true randomness, so players can reset or perform actions to always get the result they want.
how: Factor the system's internal clock or similar indefinite value into random number generation.
anti_pattern: Predictable random results that resetting can exploit.

title: Debug Mode
principle: Build debug commands for your most common test setups
why: Without certain debug features you have to spend time coming up with other solutions.
how: Add direct commands for frequent setups, like setting every fighter to a given damage percentage.
anti_pattern: Workarounds such as temporarily changing a move's damage to set up tests.
example: Before Smash had a damage-setting feature, the team set Fox's forward tilt to deal 100% damage.

title: Debug Mode
principle: Map debug functions onto the normal gameplay controller
why: Hunting down a separate debug controller whenever you need it is a real pain.
how: Assign debug functions to button combinations on the same controller used for play.
anti_pattern: A dedicated second controller for debug mode.

title: Debug Mode
principle: Keep the debug mode organized, pruned and out of the final build
why: Teams use debug mode every day, so its convenience has a huge impact on productivity, but these modes easily bloat.
how: Regularly reorganize and prune debug menus, and strip them before release.
anti_pattern: A bloated, disorganized debug menu.
quote: the convenience a debug mode provides will have a huge impact on a team's productivity.

title: Debug Mode
principle: Promote easy-to-understand debug tools into player features
why: Some debug visualizations help players learn, as long as they're easy to understand.
how: Review debug overlays for ones that could ship in a training mode, weighing whether they reveal too much.
example: Smash Bros. Training Mode's trajectory guide began as a debug feature Sakurai requested.

title: Bug Testing Systems
principle: Automate overnight CPU matches to hunt bugs in combinatorial games
why: In games with near-limitless combinations, or open worlds where players can go almost anywhere, human testing alone is far too cumbersome.
how: Run CPU-vs-CPU battles overnight to surface bugs, and near the end of the project run worldwide playtests that pass save data between regions.
example: Smash Bros. ran CPU battles all night; testers in Japan, North America and Europe passed save data back and forth.
quote: With Smash Bros., we would occasionally run CPU battles all night long to find bugs.

title: Portraying Fingers
principle: Cut finger articulation where processing is tight; spend it where it matters
why: Fingers are very complex for their size, and giving structure to every finger on a busy screen and calculating its movement costs heavily.
how: Lock finger joints so they only appear movable, swap in pre-made finger patterns when needed, and move the saved processing to more important parts.
anti_pattern: Fully simulating every finger on screens crowded with characters.
quote: Depending on the hardware and your goals, you'll constantly need to consider cutting where you can and diverting processing to the parts that matter.

title: Storage Tips
principle: Label every cable, adapter and input in your setup
why: With many consoles hooked up, cables get tangled, and labels let him tell what is plugged into the selector and which adapter goes to what.
how: Label every cable, adapter and selector input with a label printer, and route the cables together down one channel.
example: Tepra labels on the selector wiring and adapters.
quote: This way, I can tell what's plugged into the selector and which adapter goes to what.

title: Transparency Features
principle: Build a dev-mode option to make chosen model parts translucent or hidden
why: Capes and clothes hide poses, earlier workarounds like scaling or removing the cape were clumsier, and the feature didn't take long to implement.
how: Let developers select the whole model or individual parts and set them translucent or invisible while reviewing animations, including for checks outside the team.
anti_pattern: Scaling or deleting model parts just to inspect an animation.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's caped fighters; a 3D fighting game developer whose tools could disable clothes and swaying objects.
quote: While this mode is purely for developer use, I highly recommend adding transparency features if possible.

title: Transparency Features
principle: Let developers toggle each display element on or off
why: Sakurai calls per-element display toggles another must-have, and the team used them frequently.
how: Add a debug toggle for each display element so anyone can isolate exactly what they are checking.
quote: This is another must-have!

title: Computer-Controlled Players
principle: Drive action-game AI with precomputed reach, timing and opponent data
why: The computer has no eyes, so it has to decide from data about its own attack and movement ranges, the opponent's attacks, and positioning and status.
how: Convert each character's attack ranges, movement range and attack timing into data the AI can query, and give it the opponent's attack data, position and status.
quote: The computer doesn't have eyes, so it uses information from various categories.

title: Computer-Controlled Players
principle: Test layered AI behavior modes for contradictions
why: Switching logic (angry at low HP, keep optimal distance, go easy when winning) can contradict itself, and contradictions grow as mechanics and criteria multiply.
how: List the conditions each behavior mode responds to, and test the cases where two modes would choose opposite actions.
anti_pattern: Piling on behavior criteria without checking for conflicts.
quote: As such, when contradictions arise in the differing logic types, the computer player may not act properly.

title: Online Updates
principle: Plan for the market to find bugs your testers can't
why: A one-in-a-thousand bug is unlikely to show up in testing, every fix restarts checking from scratch, and after launch players put the game through far more.
how: Lock content early to get time with near-final builds, and watch player videos and reports after launch as a major test pass.
example: A bug only one in a thousand players hits can be uploaded as a video once the game is out.

title: Famicom and NES Audio
principle: Check that audio features exist on every hardware version you ship
why: The NES lacked the cartridge pins for expansion audio and the Disk System stayed in Japan, so several games' music felt different overseas.
how: List the audio features each target platform or region supports and provide fallbacks; larger ROMs later let DPCM close the gap.
anti_pattern: Relying on audio hardware only some versions have.
example: Several Famicom games sounded different from their NES versions without expansion chips.

title: The Limitations of Particle Effects
principle: Use pre-authored or pattern-based effects when processing is scarce
why: Hand-placed frame animations cost ROM but very little processing, and work within the hardware's limits.
how: Bake effects as frame animations or pick randomly from preset motion patterns, mixing light and dark pixels for visibility on any background.
example: Kirby's Dream Land: enemy-defeat stars and explosions hand-placed per frame; the inhale effect plays from set patterns.
quote: All you can do is work within your game's limits and try to aim for the best effect possible.

title: CRT Displays
principle: Treat display response time as part of how the game feels
why: CRTs need no buffer or image processor, so they respond fast, and score-chasers for classic games go out of their way to use them.
how: Test timing-critical play on the displays your players use, knowing skilled players notice the difference in response.
example: Score-chasers playing classic games on CRTs.
quote: As opposed to LCD monitors, CRTs don't require a buffer or image processor, giving them fast response time.

title: Mr. Iwata
principle: Fix bugs in the code before trying to tune parameters
why: Even with correct parameters, mistakes in the code mean almost no adjustment gives the result you want, which wasted Sakurai's time as the one tuning.
how: When tuning stops responding as expected, have programmers hunt the underlying bugs directly.
anti_pattern: Tuning parameters on top of buggy code.
example: Super Smash Bros. Melee's final stretch, when Iwata worked with the programmers to find the code problems.
quote: Even if the parameters are set correctly, if the code itself has mistakes in it, almost no amount of adjustments can make things turn out how you want.
